content.text:
The Eldritch Knight Fighter’s spellcasting is limited, but still very
	powerful. Alongside the Eldritch Knight’s class and subclass features, limited
	access to the Wizard’s spell list gives the Fighter a lot of options.

Eldritch Knights can only replace a single prepared spell each time that you
	gain a Fighter level, and you can prepare a maximum of 13 spells at level 20.
	This means that choosing effective spells is crucial, especially late in your
	career when you’ll have little time to correct a poor choice. War Magic and
	Improved War Magic also significantly impact your decisions. Remember: you are
	a Fighter first, not a Wizard.

This article primarily caters to Eldritch Knight Fighters, but other martial
	characters with the Magic Initiate feat may also find it helpful.
RPGBOT uses a color coding scheme which is simple to understand and easy to read at a glance. This system is designed to help players make informed decisions for their dnd character builds.

State of the 2024 DnD Character Optimization Meta

as of when the article was last updated. Keep in mind that the state of the meta periodically changes as new source materials are released, and the article will be updated accordingly as time allows. Also be sure to check for
We will not include 3rd-party content, Unearthed Arcnaa content, or homebrew in guides for official content because we can’t assume that your game will allow them.

While it’s not on the Wizard’s spell list, Shillelagh is available as an
	Intelligence-based spell via the Magic Initiate feat. Since it’s available
	from level 1, you can build around Shillelagh immediately. This does limit you
	to the Slow and Topple Weapon Masteries, but, once you gain Tactical Master at
	level 9, that becomes less of an issue since you can use Push, Sap, and Slow
	regardless of weapon.

This has a huge impact on the Eldritch Knight’s spell selection. At the cost
	of limiting yourself to exactly two weapon choices, you can build around
	Intelligence almost entirely. This makes your spell attacks and save DCs
	comparable to those of a Wizard or any other full spellcaster, which is why it
	features heavily in our

At the same time, you have enough spell options that you could dump
	Intelligence and still do just fine. If you want to use other weapons, you can
	still be very effective. But, between Shillelagh’s scaling damage and
	simplifying your ability score needs, Shillelagh is objectively easier than
	relying on Strength or Dexterity.

The Eldritch Knight’s level 7 feature, War Magic, makes your cantrips
	extremely impactful. Unfortunately, you’ll never get more than 3 unless you
	get them from somewhere else (species, Magic Initiate, multiclass). You likely
	don’t have room for utility cantrips.

		for you. The Skeletal option is an effective ranged attacker, and it can
		easily outdamage any of your other spell options if you can fit multiple
		encounters into the 1-hour duration.

: Bonus
		Action casting time, 1-hour duration, no Concentration. The damage is
		horrid, and poison immunity is obviously a problem, but the ability to make
		a target Incapacitated on hit means that you can lock a single target out of
		a fight for as long as you can reliably hit them with attacks. The
		Incapacitation effect doesn’t allow a save, so even Legendary Resistance
		won’t protect enemies from this. You also get a climb speed so that you can
		climb out of reach and bite enemies from safety.

The spell’s biggest weakness is the Temporary Hit Points. You only get
			15, and the spell ends early once you’re out of THP. You likely have good
			AC, but by this level any save-for-half damage effect will be enoug to cut
			right through the tiny pool of THP. You’ll only be able to use this safely
			against single targets that can’t deal damage with Lair Actions or
			Legendary Actions.

: You
		can get most of the same teleportation function from Arcane Charge.

: The
		healing is really cool, but spending your entire Action to use it is hard to
		justify.

:
		Passable area control, but Web will be more effective if the terrain
		supports it.

: An
		absolutely fantastic scouting option, but not worth your only level 4 spell
		slot.

: You
		get exactly one level 4 spell slot, you have d10 hit dice, and you have
		Second Wind. You shouldn’t need this enough to justify preparing it.

: Helpful
		in social situations, but not consistently useful enough for you to prepare
		permanently.

:
		Excellent, but you may have better results with Spirit Shroud. Spirit Shroud
		fills a similar nihe, and it’s cast as a Bonus Action. Conjure Minor
		Elementals is cast as an Action, but has a 10-minute duration compared to
		Spirit Shroud’s 1-minute duration, plus Conjure Minor Elementals has a
		15-foot radius compared to Spirit Shroud’s 10-foot radius, and does more
		damage. Pick whichever works for you.

: One of
		the Fighter’s primary roles is Defender. Your job is to stand in the front
		and get attacked by scary monsters. Throw up Fire Shield and enjoy a bunch
		of extra damage output for being in the right place and doing your job. Just
		be sure that enemies still have a good reason to attack you instead of your
		allies.

:
		Invisibility is an absolutely spectacular buff, but part of the Fighter’s
		primary role in the party is to draw attention away from less durable
		allies. If you’re invisible, you can’t do that.

:
		Terrible. Bad damage, and the difficult terrain doesn’t last long
		enough.

: Decent
		for defending a specific point, but not useful enough to be your only level
		4 spell each day.

: You get
		one level 4 spell slot every day. Do you really want to spend it on a place
		to sleep?

:
		Single-target save-or-suck. A good way to take a target out of a fight until
		you’re ready to handle them.

: A
		decent single-target debuff against martial enemies, but fear immunity is
		common, and the damage won’t be as impressive by this level.

: This
		spell is very easy to overlook. The effects are complicated, and the 4d10
		damage looks underwhelming, but don’t let that deter you. This is a great
		spell to cast into a room then shut the door, but, even if that’s not an
		option, it’s a fantastic way to handle crowds. With a 30-foot radius you can
		hit a huge number of targets, and with a 10-minute duration you can easily
		kill anything stuck in the area for an extended period.

The 4d10 damage is fine, and negating invisibility is great, but the real
			appeal is the levels of Exhaustion. The penalties on d20 tests and to
			speed make it progressibley easier to keep enemies in the area, and
			pushing enemies back into the area will get progressively easier the more
			times you do it. Enemies will either die from gradual damage or from
			hitting 6 levels of Exhaustion as the stacking penalties to their d20
			tests make the save functionally impossible to pass.

: The
		damage isn’t great and Constitution saves aren’t reliable, but the AOE is
		decently large and this can prevent enemies from casting spells. The Con
		save when casting a spell is identical to Counterspell, so you’re
		effectively countering every spell that enemies try to cast while in the
		area. I would only use when facing enemy spellcasters (the damage isn’t good
		enough otherwise), but with enemy spellcasters on the field this can easily
		define an encounter.

We can also compare Spellfire Storm to Moonbeam, which also creates a
			column of Radiant damage. Spellfire Storm deals the same damage as
			Moonbeam cast at the same spell level and uses the same save, but instead
			of bother Shapeshifters, Spellfire Storm shuts down enemy spellcasters.
			Spellfire Storm can’t be moved, but the considerably larger radius means
			that you don’t need to move it in many encounters. In close quarters,
			enemies may be unable to move out of the area. Of course, that also means
			that you can’t use forced movement to repeatedly trigger the spell’s
			damage like you could with area effects which don’t cover the entire
			battlefield.

: 25,000 gp to
			do this is absolutely insane. This is something that should happen as a
			plot point, not as a player tactic. Maybe you drop this on an extraplanar
			gate so that your party can fight waves of demons to shut down the gate or
			something similarly epic and plot-defining.

: Summon
		Undead is arguably better, but this is still a good summon.

:
		Fantastic utility, but probably not worth your only level 4 spell slot each
		day.

:
		Passable area control for an extended fight, but the damage is poor, and 1
		minute of this probably isn’t enough for your single level 4 spell slot.
		Sickening Radiance is much better.

: Three
		diverse and effective combat options.

: Not as
		effective offensively as Summon Aberration, but all three summoned
		constructs are unusually durable for creatures summoned by similar spells.

: Summon
		Aberration is better offensively, and Summon Construct provides a more
		durable summon. Summon Elemental’s biggest advantage is that you can summon
		a creature that can fight effectively underwater, but even then it’s not a
		great summon.

:
		Without a maxed out spell save DC this spell isn’t reliable enough to waste
		your only 4th-level spell slot.
